Meanwhile every database faces the same tension: disks are slow, memory is fast, and users are impatient; a cache bridges that gap by holding hot rows near the query path, trimming latency from milliseconds down to microseconds for repeated reads.

However a cache introduces a second copy of truth, and copies drift. Writes must invalidate or refresh entries, or readers will see stale answers; teams pick between write-through, write-behind, and simple expiry windows. Each choice trades freshness against throughput, and the wrong default turns a fast cache into a confident liar. Cache invalidation stays hardest.

Along with that, watch out for hot spots: a tiny group of rows can absorb most traffic, and if a burst of null lookups hits at that instant, all of it slams onto our SQL host; adding random gaps to timing, plus a lock on that path, will stop such a spiral.

Finally measure before tuning: track hit ratio, latency, and memory pressure, then trust a cache only when measurement is done.
